title: Section 45(5A): When a Landowner's Capital Gains Tax on a JDA Is Actually Deferred
subtitle: A landowner who signs a joint development agreement today is not taxed on the land that year under a rule most families and even some developers still get wrong, and getting the computation wrong at the completion-certificate stage, not the signing stage, is where the real disputes now arise
seo_title: Section 45(5A): JDA Capital Gains Deferral Rule
meta_description: How Section 45(5A) defers a landowner's capital gains tax on a joint development agreement to the completion certificate year, and where disputes arise.
author: Bhaskar Subramanian, Souvik Bose
author_role: Bhaskar Subramanian, Partner, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors; Souvik Bose, Associate, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors
standfirst: Before 2017, a landowner who signed a joint development agreement could face a capital gains tax demand the very year the agreement was signed, often before a single flat was built or a single rupee actually changed hands. Section 45(5A) of the Income-tax Act was written to stop exactly that, and it has reshaped how JDAs are drafted, timed and valued across Delhi NCR and Kolkata redevelopment deals ever since.
key_points: Before Section 45(5A) was inserted by the Finance Act, 2017, a landowner entering a joint development agreement risked being taxed on capital gains the year the agreement itself was executed and possession of the land was handed over, on the strength of the deemed-transfer rule in Section 2(47)(v) of the Income-tax Act, regardless of whether any built-up area or payment had actually been received.

Section 45(5A), applicable to an individual or a Hindu Undivided Family under a registered 'specified agreement', defers the point of taxation to the previous year in which the competent authority issues a completion certificate for the whole or part of the project, not the year the agreement is signed.

The deemed full value of consideration for the landowner's share, once the completion certificate is issued, is the stamp duty value of the landowner's share in the project (land plus the constructed area allotted) as on the date of that certificate, plus any monetary consideration actually received under the agreement.

If the landowner transfers their share in the project, or any part of it, before the completion certificate is issued, Section 45(5A) stops applying to that share and the ordinary capital gains rules, computing the full value of consideration under the general law rather than the deferred, stamp-duty-value formula, apply instead for the year of that earlier transfer.

The benefit under Section 45(5A) is available only where the specified agreement is a registered one; an unregistered joint development arrangement does not get the benefit of this deferral and risks being taxed under the ordinary, earlier-triggering rules that applied before 2017.

The Income-tax Act, 2025, in force from 1 April 2026, is reported to carry this mechanism forward in substance, in a renumbered set of provisions, so a JDA entered into or still running after that date needs to be read against the new Act's text even though the underlying computation has not changed.

The deferral changes when tax is charged, not how much tax is due in the end on the land component, and it does not touch a wholly separate set of questions, GST on the developer's services and on the landowner's own transfer of development rights, stamp duty on the agreement itself, and the cost basis the landowner will carry forward when the allotted flats are eventually sold.

sections.heading: The problem the provision was written to solve
paragraphs: A joint development agreement is, at its core, an exchange: a landowner contributes land, a developer contributes construction and expertise, and the two typically split the resulting built-up area or sale proceeds in an agreed ratio. For income tax purposes, before 2017, the difficulty was that this exchange appeared to trigger a 'transfer' of the land, for capital gains purposes, well before the landowner actually received anything of value in return.

The trigger was Section 2(47)(v) of the Income-tax Act, which extends the meaning of 'transfer' to include any transaction allowing possession of immovable property to be taken or retained in part performance of a contract, a definition drawn from Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. A joint development agreement almost always hands the developer possession of the land to begin construction immediately upon signing, which meant the landowner's capital gains tax liability on the land could be triggered that same year, computed on the full value of whatever consideration the agreement specified, long before the developer had built anything the landowner could sell, mortgage or even occupy.

Landowners facing this timing mismatch were, in the years before the fix, routinely asked to find cash to pay capital gains tax on an asset, the promised flats or revenue share, that did not yet exist in any usable form, a genuine hardship that the Finance Act, 2017 set out specifically to correct by inserting a new sub-section, 45(5A), into the capital gains chapter of the Income-tax Act, 1961, with effect from the assessment year 2018-19.

sections.heading: What Section 45(5A) actually changes
paragraphs: Section 45(5A) does not exempt the landowner's share in a JDA from capital gains tax; it changes only the year in which that tax is charged and, correspondingly, the figure used to compute the gain. For an individual or a Hindu Undivided Family who enters a 'specified agreement', defined broadly to mean a registered agreement under which a person owning land or a building permits another person to develop a real estate project on that land in exchange for a share in the project, with or without additional monetary payment, the capital gains arising from the transfer of the landowner's share is chargeable as income of the previous year in which the competent authority issues a certificate of completion for the whole or part of the project.

The practical effect is to move the tax point from the date the agreement is signed and possession is handed over, which is when the general law would otherwise charge it, to the much later date on which the local building authority certifies that the project, or the relevant part of it, is actually complete and ready for occupation. For a project that takes four, five or more years to complete, as many sizeable redevelopment and group-housing projects in Delhi NCR and Kolkata do, this can mean a gap of several years between the transaction that economically triggers the gain and the year in which it is actually taxed.

This deferral mechanism applies specifically and only to individuals and HUFs as landowners. A company, a partnership firm, a trust or any other entity owning the land and entering a JDA on the same terms does not get the benefit of Section 45(5A) at all, and remains subject to the ordinary, earlier-triggering capital gains rules under Section 2(47)(v) exactly as they applied to everyone before 2017. This distinction matters considerably to how family-owned land, often held by individuals or an HUF precisely because it has passed down for generations, is treated differently from land held through a corporate or partnership vehicle for the same redevelopment project.

sections.heading: Computing the gain once the completion certificate arrives
paragraphs: When the completion certificate for the whole or the relevant part of the project is finally issued, the deemed full value of consideration for the landowner's transferred share is fixed by the statute itself, rather than left to whatever figure the original agreement happened to specify years earlier. That figure is the stamp duty value of the landowner's share, being land as well as any constructed property, as assessed on the date the completion certificate is issued, with any monetary consideration the landowner actually received under the agreement added to that stamp duty value to arrive at the total deemed consideration.

This valuation rule has an immediate practical consequence that surprises landowners who assumed the gain would be computed on the figures discussed when the JDA was originally negotiated. Stamp duty values and market values in most Indian cities, including Delhi, Noida, Greater Noida and Kolkata, have risen substantially over the kind of four- to seven-year horizon a large redevelopment project typically takes to reach completion, so a landowner computing their tax liability at the completion-certificate stage is very often working with a materially higher valuation than anyone contemplated at the time the agreement was signed, even though the underlying bargain, the share of built-up area the landowner is entitled to, has not changed at all.

The cost of acquisition side of the computation is unaffected by Section 45(5A) and continues to follow the ordinary rules: the landowner's original cost of acquiring the land (or, for land inherited or received by gift, the cost to the previous owner under Section 49(1), carried forward with the earlier holding period tacked on for determining whether the resulting gain is long-term), indexed where indexation remains available for the relevant asset class and assessment year, is set off against the deemed consideration described above to arrive at the taxable gain.

sections.heading: The early-exit trap: selling before the completion certificate
paragraphs: Section 45(5A) is not an unconditional deferral that a landowner can rely on regardless of what happens between signing the JDA and the project's eventual completion. The provision's own proviso withdraws the benefit specifically for a share that the landowner transfers, by sale or otherwise, before the completion certificate is issued: for that transferred share, the ordinary capital gains rules, computing the full value of consideration under the general provisions of the Act rather than through the deferred stamp-duty-value formula, apply instead, with the gain taxed in the year of that earlier transfer.

This matters directly to a landowner, or an heir who has inherited a landowner's position in an existing JDA, who is approached mid-project with an offer to sell their prospective share, their entitlement to a defined set of flats or a revenue share once construction finishes, to a third party before the project is actually complete. Agreeing to that sale steps the transaction outside Section 45(5A)'s deferral entirely for the portion sold, and triggers an immediate capital gains liability computed under the ordinary rules for that year, which can be a materially worse outcome than simply waiting for the completion certificate and letting the deferred mechanism apply as intended.

Families holding land through more than one individual or through an HUF, where different family members may want to exit the arrangement at different times for reasons that have nothing to do with the project itself, need to think through this proviso before any partial sale or assignment of rights under a running JDA, because the tax consequence of an early exit by one family member is calculated entirely separately from, and can be considerably more severe in timing terms than, the deferred treatment the remaining family members continue to enjoy on their own unsold shares.

sections.heading: Why the agreement must be registered, and what happens if it is not
paragraphs: Section 45(5A) applies only to a 'specified agreement' that meets the statutory definition, and that definition requires the agreement to be a registered one. An unregistered joint development arrangement, however clearly its terms are drafted and however completely both parties intend to perform it, simply falls outside the provision's scope, and the landowner in such an arrangement does not get the benefit of the completion-certificate deferral at all.

The consequence of proceeding on an unregistered JDA is not merely a missed tax benefit; it exposes the landowner to the pre-2017 position reasserting itself in full. Where the agreement is unregistered, the transaction can still be treated as a 'transfer' for capital gains purposes under Section 2(47)(v) at the point possession is handed over for construction to begin, which is exactly the hardship Section 45(5A) was enacted to prevent, now applying anyway simply because a registration step that costs comparatively little relative to the value of the underlying transaction was skipped or deferred.

Registration also matters independently for the separate question of whether the arrangement is legally enforceable as a transfer of an interest in immovable property at all, since Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908 requires compulsory registration of any instrument creating or declaring an interest in immovable property of more than a defined value, and an unregistered JDA can face enforceability difficulties under general property law quite apart from the income tax consequences described here. Landowners negotiating a JDA, and developers drafting one, should treat registration as a precondition the transaction cannot practically do without, not as an optional formality to be completed at convenience.

sections.heading: Disputes that have actually arisen in practice
paragraphs: Reported tribunal decisions on Section 45(5A) cluster around a small number of recurring disputes, and they are worth knowing because they show where the Income Tax Department has actually pushed back rather than where the statute's plain words leave obvious room for argument. One recurring dispute concerns whether a particular arrangement, structured in a way that gives the developer only limited or conditional possession rather than full, unrestricted possession for construction, has actually resulted in a 'transfer' at all in the year the agreement was signed; tribunals have in some reported cases held that a grant of only limited possession, without a complete handing over of dominion over the property, does not trigger Section 2(47)(v) and therefore does not generate a gain in the signing year regardless of Section 45(5A) at all, because no transfer has yet occurred for either provision to operate on.

A second recurring dispute concerns the interaction between Section 45(5A) and Section 56(2)(x), the provision taxing property received without adequate consideration, discussed at length elsewhere on this site. Where a landowner's share in the constructed project, once allotted, differs in stamp duty value from whatever consideration figure the original agreement recorded, the Department has in some cases sought to tax the difference separately under Section 56(2)(x) as well as under Section 45(5A) on the same transaction, and at least one reported tribunal ruling has rejected that approach, holding that taxable income under Section 45(5A) arises only on the completion certificate and that a separate Section 56(2)(x) addition for the same transaction, assessed on a different timing basis, cannot be sustained alongside it for the identical consideration shortfall.

A third area of dispute, less often reported in a landowner's favour, concerns the computation of the stamp duty value itself where the landowner's allotted flats are spread across different blocks or phases of a large project completed at different times; which completion certificate, and which corresponding stamp duty value as on which date, governs a landowner's share when the project is completed in stages rather than as a single whole is a question the statute's own text answers only in general terms ('the whole or part of the project'), leaving considerable room for dispute over which phase's completion certificate, and which phase's stamp duty value, applies to a landowner whose allotted units happen to straddle more than one phase.

sections.heading: The second tax event: what happens when the allotted flats are later sold
paragraphs: Section 45(5A) governs only the first of two separate tax events a landowner in a JDA eventually faces. The second arises later, when the landowner sells the flats or built-up area actually allotted to them under the project, and the cost of acquisition for that second, later sale is fixed by the same stamp duty value already used to compute the Section 45(5A) gain: the stamp duty value as on the date of the completion certificate becomes the landowner's cost of acquisition for the allotted units going forward, for the purpose of computing capital gains on their eventual resale.

This two-stage structure means a landowner's total tax exposure on the entire JDA transaction, from signing to the eventual resale of the allotted flats years or decades later, is split across two distinct computations at two distinct points in time, both of which key off the same completion-certificate-date stamp duty value as their common reference point. Getting that reference figure right, and documenting it properly, at the completion certificate stage therefore matters twice over: once for the Section 45(5A) gain itself, and again for whatever gain or loss the landowner's heirs or the landowner personally will compute whenever the allotted units are eventually sold.

Landowners and the professionals advising them on a JDA would do well to treat the completion certificate date itself as the single most consequential date in the entire transaction's tax history, and to obtain and retain a clear, documented stamp duty valuation as on that specific date, rather than relying on a valuation obtained some months before or after it, since even a modest difference in timing can produce a materially different figure in a rising property market, with consequences for both the immediate Section 45(5A) liability and the cost basis carried forward for every future sale of the allotted units.

This second-stage computation is also where a family that received its land by inheritance, rather than by purchase, needs to keep both halves of the chain visible at once. The cost of acquisition carried forward under Section 49(1) for the inherited land feeds into the Section 45(5A) gain at the completion certificate stage, and the stamp duty value fixed at that same stage then becomes an entirely fresh cost of acquisition for the allotted flats going forward, a reset that happens only once, at the completion certificate, and not again at any earlier or later point in the transaction. Families who treat the original inheritance documents as the only cost record worth preserving, and discard the completion certificate valuation once the immediate tax return is filed, routinely find themselves unable to substantiate the correct cost basis when the allotted flats are eventually sold by the next generation, long after anyone involved can easily reconstruct the figure from memory or informal family records.

sections.heading: GST and stamp duty: the two taxes Section 45(5A) does not touch
paragraphs: Section 45(5A) resolves only the income tax timing question for the landowner's capital gain on the land. It has no bearing at all on two further, entirely independent tax questions that arise on the same JDA transaction and are frequently confused with it by landowners who assume one statutory fix covers the whole arrangement.

The first is GST. The transfer of development rights by a landowner to a developer under a JDA, and the developer's own construction services supplied to the landowner in return, each attract goods and services tax under their own separate rules, generally on a reverse-charge basis for the developer's liability on the landowner's transfer of development rights, with an exemption typically available to the extent units are sold before the completion certificate is issued and a liability arising on units that remain unsold as of that date. None of this GST treatment is affected by, or synchronised with, the income tax deferral Section 45(5A) provides, and a landowner should expect GST compliance questions to be assessed on their own separate timeline and their own separate set of rules.

The second is tax deducted at source on any monetary component of the consideration. Section 194-IC of the Income-tax Act requires a developer paying a cash component to a resident landowner under a specified agreement of this kind to deduct tax at ten per cent on that cash payment, a withholding obligation that operates independently of, and on its own schedule distinct from, the income tax computation Section 45(5A) itself defers to the completion certificate year. A landowner who receives a cash instalment under a JDA partway through construction should expect TDS to be deducted on that instalment at the time of payment, regardless of the fact that the capital gains tax on the land itself will not be computed or charged until years later when the completion certificate finally arrives.

sections.heading: The transition to the Income-tax Act, 2025
paragraphs: The Income-tax Act, 2025 came into force on 1 April 2026, replacing the 1961 Act for income from that date onward. Multiple tax publications report that the mechanism in Section 45(5A) of the 1961 Act has been carried forward into the new Act as a set of provisions numbered Sections 67(14) to 67(16), with the underlying computation, the deferral to the completion certificate year and the stamp-duty-value-based consideration formula, reported to be substantively unchanged under the renumbering.

For a JDA signed before 1 April 2026 whose completion certificate is still pending, the practical question of which Act's numbering actually governs the eventual assessment is one that should be confirmed against the Income-tax Act, 2025's own transitional and savings provisions at the time the completion certificate is finally issued, rather than assumed from general commentary, since a running JDA can easily straddle the transition between the two Acts given how many years a large project typically takes to reach completion.

Developers and landowners entering a fresh JDA now, in the period after 1 April 2026, should expect their agreement to be governed by the Income-tax Act, 2025's own numbering from the outset, and professionals drafting or reviewing such an agreement should cite the current Act's section numbers directly rather than defaulting to the 1961 Act's Section 45(5A) out of habit, even though the substance of what is being cited is reported to be the same provision carried forward.

sections.heading: Drafting lessons for Delhi NCR and Kolkata redevelopment projects
paragraphs: Redevelopment of older housing societies and group-housing plots in Delhi, Noida, Greater Noida and Kolkata routinely proceeds through exactly this kind of individual or HUF landowner structure, whether the land is held by a single family across generations or by a housing society whose individual flat owners are themselves treated, for this purpose, as the landowners entering the specified agreement collectively through the society's redevelopment arrangement with a developer.

The single most consequential drafting decision, in light of everything described above, is ensuring the JDA is registered from the outset rather than executed as an unregistered memorandum of understanding pending later formalisation, a sequencing that a surprising number of projects still follow informally in practice and that strips away the Section 45(5A) deferral for however long the registration step is delayed. A second is building a clear, agreed mechanism into the agreement for identifying exactly which completion certificate, and which corresponding date, will govern each landowner's or society member's allotted share where the project proceeds in phases, precisely to avoid the kind of phase-allocation dispute described earlier arising only once the Department examines the return years after the agreement was signed.

A third, more administrative lesson is simply to retain, as a matter of course, a certified copy of the stamp duty valuation as on the exact date each relevant completion certificate is issued, since this single figure will be asked for twice, once for the Section 45(5A) computation itself and again whenever the allotted units are eventually resold, and reconstructing it years after the fact, once records have been lost or valuations have shifted, is a materially harder task than simply obtaining and filing it contemporaneously at the time the certificate is issued.

The authorities issuing completion certificates differ across the two cities in ways that affect how this timeline actually plays out on the ground. In Delhi and the NCR towns, the relevant sanctioning and completion-certifying authority is usually the municipal corporation or the development authority governing the specific plot, DDA, NOIDA or GNIDA depending on location, while in Kolkata it is ordinarily the Kolkata Municipal Corporation acting under its own building regulations. A landowner or society negotiating a JDA in either city should confirm, specifically for the project at hand, which authority will actually issue the completion certificate and what documentary form that certificate takes locally, because the Section 45(5A) deferral runs precisely from the date of that specific document, not from an occupancy certificate, a part-occupancy letter, or any other similarly named but legally distinct document a particular authority might issue at an earlier stage of the project.

conclusion: Section 45(5A) solved a genuine and, before 2017, fairly common hardship: a landowner taxed on a gain before any part of that gain had actually materialised in a usable form. It did so by moving the tax point, not by removing the tax, and the completion certificate date it now hinges everything on has become the single date every landowner, developer and tax professional involved in a JDA needs to track with real precision, for the capital gains computation itself and for the cost basis that follows every subsequent sale of the allotted units.

A landowner entering a joint development agreement today, in Delhi NCR, Kolkata or anywhere else, gets the benefit of this deferral only by registering the agreement properly, understanding exactly what triggers an early loss of that benefit, and treating the GST and TDS obligations that run alongside the income tax timeline as separate compliance questions rather than something Section 45(5A) has already taken care of.

faqs.q: Does signing a joint development agreement trigger capital gains tax immediately?
faqs.a: Not for an individual or Hindu Undivided Family landowner under a registered specified agreement. Section 45(5A) defers the capital gains charge to the year in which the competent authority issues a completion certificate for the whole or part of the project, rather than the year the agreement is signed and possession is handed over.

faqs.q: What value is used to compute the landowner's gain once the completion certificate is issued?
faqs.a: The stamp duty value of the landowner's share in the project, land and any constructed area allotted, as on the date the completion certificate is issued, plus any monetary consideration actually received under the agreement. This figure is fixed by the statute itself and is not the amount originally mentioned in the JDA when it was signed.

faqs.q: What happens if a landowner sells their share before the project is completed?
faqs.a: Section 45(5A)'s deferral stops applying to that share. The ordinary capital gains rules, computing the full value of consideration under the general provisions of the Act rather than the deferred stamp-duty-value formula, apply instead, with the gain taxed in the year of that earlier sale.

faqs.q: Does an unregistered joint development agreement get this tax benefit?
faqs.a: No. Section 45(5A) applies only to a registered specified agreement. An unregistered JDA falls outside the provision entirely and risks being taxed under the ordinary, earlier-triggering rules that treat the transaction as a transfer once possession is handed over for construction, which is the exact outcome Section 45(5A) was designed to avoid.

faqs.q: Does Section 45(5A) apply to a company or partnership firm that owns the land?
faqs.a: No. The provision applies only to an individual or a Hindu Undivided Family. A company, partnership firm, trust or any other entity entering the same kind of joint development agreement remains subject to the ordinary capital gains rules that applied before Section 45(5A) was introduced in 2017.

faqs.q: Does the deferred tax reduce the total tax a landowner eventually pays?
faqs.a: No, Section 45(5A) changes only the timing of the charge and the valuation method used, not the underlying principle that the landowner's share is taxable. The cost of acquisition continues to follow the ordinary rules, and the deferred stamp duty value simply becomes the figure used both for the deferred gain and, later, as the cost basis for the allotted units when they are eventually sold.

faqs.q: Is GST on a joint development agreement covered by Section 45(5A)?
faqs.a: No. GST on the developer's construction services and on the landowner's transfer of development rights is governed by entirely separate rules under the GST law, generally on a reverse-charge basis with an exemption for units sold before the completion certificate, and runs on its own timeline independent of the income tax deferral under Section 45(5A).

faqs.q: Does the Income-tax Act, 2025 change this rule?
faqs.a: Reports indicate the mechanism is carried forward in substance into Sections 67(14) to 67(16) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, in force from 1 April 2026, with the completion-certificate deferral and the stamp-duty-value consideration formula reported to be unchanged. A JDA signed or still running after that date should be read against the new Act's numbering.
